Whether you join me for a research internship, an end-of-studies project or a master's thesis, a large part of what makes an internship successful is not technical: it is how we **work together**. Here are the habits I ask of every intern. They will serve you well in any company or laboratory.

## Before a meeting: send an agenda

Send a short agenda **the day before** each meeting (by email or in our shared folder). It should list:

- the **purpose** of the meeting;
- the **points** to discuss, in order of priority;
- for each point, what you expect: information, a discussion, or a **decision**;
- the documents to read beforehand, with a link.

An agenda makes you prepare, lets me prepare too, and keeps the meeting focused on what matters.

## During a meeting: lead it with slides

**Always prepare a few slides** to lead the meeting, even for a 30-minute weekly point. It is your meeting: you lead it.

- Start with a reminder of the objectives and of what was decided last time.
- Show what you did since the last meeting: results, figures, tables — not just text.
- Present the difficulties you met and the **questions** you need answered.
- End with the next steps you propose.

Slides force you to structure your thinking, and they give us a shared support to discuss, annotate and decide on. They also build, week after week, the material for your final presentation.

## After a meeting: write the minutes

Send the **minutes of meeting (MoM)** within 24 hours. They do not need to be long:

| Item | Content |
|---|---|
| Date and participants | Who was there |
| Decisions | What we decided, and why if useful |
| Actions | **Who** does **what**, by **when** |
| Open questions | What remains to be clarified |
| Next meeting | Date and expected topics |

The minutes are our common memory. They avoid misunderstandings, and the action list becomes the starting point of the next agenda.

## Manage your files online and share them

Work in a **shared cloud folder** from day one (the one we agree on at the start: the university's cloud, a shared drive, or a Git repository for code).

- **Organise** the folder: for example `01_admin`, `02_literature`, `03_data`, `04_code`, `05_results`, `06_meetings`, `07_report`.
- **Name files clearly** and consistently, with the date first: `2026-11-18_meeting-slides.pptx`, `2026-11-18_MoM.docx`.
- **Never work only on your laptop**: if it breaks, your work must not disappear with it.
- **Version** your work: keep important versions, and use Git for code.
- **Keep your raw data untouched** and document every transformation, so that your results can be reproduced.
- **Respect confidentiality**: company data stay in the space agreed with the company.

## A few more habits

- **Keep a logbook**: what you did each day, what you tried, what worked and what did not. It saves hours when writing the report.
- **Ask questions early.** Being stuck for two days on a problem that a five-minute discussion would solve is a waste of your internship.
- **Manage your bibliography from the start** — see [Managing your bibliography](../2026-11-18-bibliography-for-students/index.qmd).
- **Write as you go**: draft the method and data sections of your report as soon as they are stable.

These habits take a little time each week, and save a lot of it overall. They also show your future employers that you know how to work in a team.
